utterances.text: I understand. South of the river there, that is the PTT, I believe. I confirm that is OP4, so the only debate here is to exactly what was 866587. And therefore, one questions whether, in the report written by Thomas Hansen, whether that grid was, after all, meant to illustrate what was thought to be a launch point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able now to identify for us grid reference 866587.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I have a Sarajevo map here, 1 to 50.000 scale, and 8665845 is the PTT building. I think there is a slight discrepancy on those grids.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Wing Commander, would you be able to give us the grid reference for the point which is now marked 866587? What would be the correct grid reference in your view of this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the map here, 866587 is approximately here. I still maintain that 866587 is approximately the grid of the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, let's move to Exhibit P519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, let me -- I don't think I got an answer to my question. What in the wing commander's view would be the correct grid reference of the northernmost of the three-points? Are you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I look at the map I have here with OP4 located on it, the northernmost point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. Sorry. The northernmost point of the three. The one that is now marked grid reference 866, incorrectly as we understand, and my question to you: What would be the correct grid reference for that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Just north of the river ... I have a map here with a number of grids overlayed. Please just give me a second. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Take your time, Officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Just to confirm, then, this spot here, this grid reference, 866587, is pretty accurate. The PTT grid, slightly further south, I would argue from this map is 864865583, 584. So that grid is correct. That grid is obviously slightly further south which I just read out. OP4 is correct. So the question is, what was that referring to that 866587, in my mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But the important thing is to establish that the indication of this grid reference, which I have come to call the northernmost of the three, this one, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The grid reference indicated on the map is correct. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is quite detailed. I'd like to know whether at the time in Sarajevo when you were drafting the report these grid reference, were they noted on some -- some kind of map that was easier to use? When you write down grid references in a report, how do you check that the grid reference is accurate? Could you tell us how you proceeded as UNMO at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, having gone into the PTT headquarters building after the event, we would have looked at the operations map in the operations room, and from our practical knowledge of the ground, our own familiarity with the ground we would have worked out whatever grid we had to do, whether that was what we perceived as being a launch point or an impact point or whatever. And that would have been recorded at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This map that was in the OPs room, was it a big map, very accurate with all these figures? Because it is quite puzzling to have all these figures on a map, so was it easy to interpret when you saw this big map?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Of course. It is it standard military mapping and there would have been a lot of detail on it. Any military map has a lot of detail, but there is nothing confusing about it. It is day-to-day business.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, fine, thank you. Let's move to document 519 then. You saw earlier the document that we looked at some pages in this document. I tried to figure out -- tried to figure out what happened that day. So could you please confirm that this will correspond to what you recollect. I know 12 years have gone by. It is a difficult exercise. But this is what must have happened. Early in the morning of the 28th this event occurred, this event that -- which Thomas Hansen makes reference to in this special report that is on the screen. So first we have the event, right, early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Then according to your recollection, around 6.00 that day at 18 hours there was conflict between Thomas Hansen and the ABiH LOs Nermin Silajdzic and Mr. Goro. Is that what happened, is that what you recollect?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I don't recall their names but if you tell me that is who the LOs were, then yes, I believe that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the document says so, on page 8 of the document that we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have page 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On page 8, I hope you see it on the screen. Could you please confirm that a meeting was held on June 29, 1995 at 4.30 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: That is what the report says, so I assume that is correct. I was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you see the names of the people attending this meeting. So that was my next question. You were not present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: However, we can continue to read on, and we see who attended this meeting, Mr. Hansen, Major Tariq, Major Sundquest, and on the other side we had the LOs Captain Nermin Silajdzic, Captain Goro, and another person whose name is unknown and this was also an interpreter. That's it, right? So what I would like to obtain from you, because you wrote your own report on July 4th, so you confirm that did you that, a week later. A week after the event, you wrote your own report. You can confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: That is the report we saw earlier today, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So all this business was reported to Zagreb on July 5th, and we could go back to page 1 of this document and here we see that the report on this investigation regarding the UNMOs and the Bosnian LOs, so all this was sent as a report on July 5th to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: If that is what you have a copy of, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: It seems a bit formal, but for the transcript, you know, I want you to confirm things, because I'm not testifying from the bar, you know, you're supposed to testify, so you are supposed to answer all these questions that might sound a bit silly at first, but it's for the transcript so everything is written down. So I apologise in advance because I'm asking you to do something that is quite difficult, you know, 12 years back. But please, could you cast your mind 12 years back. What is the first thing that springs to mind now, without looking at your notes, please? Because later you may look at your notes to refresh your memory. But out of the blue, you know, casting your mind 12 years back, what comes to mind when you think about what happened on that day in June in the summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: If I may, please, just to clarify, I take your point about the date of this report, the 5th of July, which of course I did not author nor have I seen it. But that might be a week after the event, but of course that is a weekly report going up to Zagreb from the headquarters. The day of the event, the 29th of June, is when Captain Hansen did make the report. It was made the same day. Does that clarify, to help?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But I would like to you answer my question. Twelve years after the event, more than 12 years, because we're in September now, what's the first thing that comes to your mind when you think about all these events?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I recall being in the PTT car park that morning, as I have said earlier. I believe I was with Thomas Hansen and I'm surprised to hear he recalls that we weren't together and he was inside the building, but regardless of that, I recall us watching the trajectory of some sort of projectile that came from the north north-west area crossing to our front, and as I recollect and as we believed at that time, appeared to impact in the TV building. It is conceivable it might have crossed behind, but either way, within seconds there was explosion, a detonation of -- of something. And that is my recollection of the initial event and then everything else of course follows on from there, with subsequent meetings and reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the time being that is correct's enough. For me, I'm going proceed now, we have seen a number of documents here and it appears that you were asked to draft a document related to Captain Hansen. You did that on the 4th of July. We saw this document because the Prosecutor showed you this document, confronted you with this document. This is at page 6. We have a report dated the 4th of July, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes, I was just going to confirm on the 4th of July, that is when I catalogued the incident at the meeting I went to later that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hawking.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, when Commander Knowles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm calling you Mr. -- I'm sorry I'm calling you Mr. Hawking. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I answer to anything, Your Honours. Wing Commander Knowles is referring to a number of notes, and I just wonder for the record, can we know what these are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. All I have done is print off back in the UK the attachments that were sent to me in the e-mail and I have a copy of the UNMO sector headquarters report that Captain Hansen sent up to headquarters, I have a copy of the report that I produced that you just referred to on the 4th of July, and have I a copy of the e-mail with Barry Hogan. That is all I have. And all three of those have already been on the screen this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So as not to disturb Mr. Docherty, I would like to ask to you leave your notes aside. It's just a suggestion. I'll show you the document on screen because I see that Mr. Docherty is concerned. I don't think there is any reason for that. Well, thank you very much. Thank you very much, Witness. You have your report on the screen. You can read it. Everyone can read it. It is an exhibit in this case. Well, this report, you wrote it on the 4th of July. It is about a week after the event. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to put a number of propositions to you and in order not to spend too much time on this, can you please answer by yes or no, tell me if you agree or not. On the 29th, on the 29th there is a meeting with Mr. Silajdzic and Goro on the one side and the UNMOs on the other side. The meeting takes place on that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: If you're referring to me being the UNMO going down to see them, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wondering if the meeting took place on the 28th or the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 29th. That is mentioned in the document. It is a meeting that took place following the conflictual meeting that took place between the LOs and Thomas Hansen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the following day.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following day at 4.30 p.m. That is mentioned at page 8 of the document we have on screen at the moment, P519.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that on the very day of this incident there was this conflict, conflictual meeting, you took part in part of this. So what was your share of the dispute or the conflict with Mr. Silajdzic and Mr. Goro, the LOs at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I had no conflict with them at all initially. What had happened earlier in the day had already happened. Captain Hansen had had a very aggressive meeting and was thrown out of that office and I know that because he told me. I went down to see the LOs later in the day and it says there late afternoon, 1730, and I don't recall whether I was going to try and follow up the earlier meeting that Captain Hansen had got nowhere with or if I had been tasked to go and speak about something different. Either way, as soon as I arrived in their office they were clearly still very, very angry and started telling me what had happened with Captain Hansen and the fact they were going to declare him persona non grata, et cetera. So whatever intent I had was hijacked and the meeting became a very short angry exchange as I tried to placate them because I had a reason to be there obviously and they were just being very aggressive and angry and the meeting went nowhere and I left to report to Captain Hansen what had been said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just let me have this clarified. When you say that he was thrown out, you're speaking figuratively, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, yes. He made no progress and was basically ordered to leave in a very angry fashion. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Silajdzic and Goro, did they carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I would imagine so. Everybody carried a weapon. But there is no suggestion there was any threatening behaviour using weapons, no, not at all. A side-arm is normal. Everybody has a side-arm. Not us the UNMOs but Serbian, BiH officers will carry a side-arm of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the streets of Sarajevo. Do you mean that everyone was carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. There was a war going on. People that were combatants carried weapons. The UN, UNPROFOR, us, the UNMOs, we were not armed. We did not, but UNPROFOR soldiers doing UNPROFOR convoy escort tasks they would be armed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you UNMOs were not armed?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: No, and that is the very reason and the very premise under which UNMOs are successful and operate, because by not being armed, one has freedom of movement normally. UNMOs do not present a threat to combatants on either side and therefore if an attack were to be carried out against an unarmed UNMO, well it's a murderous attack. So the strength of the UNMO organisation is the fact you don't present a threat, because you are not armed yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But there were all these armed people were sometimes very aggressive. In these circumstances, did you sometimes feel threatened?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: At page 1 of the document, but we don't have page 1 on the screen. Now we do. Mr. Alam has signed the report and it says at paragraph 1, and I'd like to ask everyone to read this first paragraph. Page 2, actually, under conclusion, we have a title recommendations, conclusion, recommendations, point 3, and I would like you to read this paragraph and to comment this paragraph. I suppose that Mr. Alam was your superior officer. He was one who sent the report to Zagreb. Please read out point 3 of this document under the title conclusions, recommendations, please, can you read out loud point 3. Starting with the word "however."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Para 3 states: "However, on the other hand it is important to point out the dangers if the issue is not resolved amicably and soon enough. These are considerable, if not complete, lack of cooperation from the ABiH with the UNMOs and increasing restrictions of movement, ROM, already we have considerable restrictions of movement within the AOR, the area of responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like us to talk about that period between the 28th in the morning and the 5th of July. We are talking about one week. Was it a very agitated or animated week?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Not that I recall, no more than any other week. The city was in a very difficult position. There was fairly regular artillery, direct tank fire rounds impacting in the city. We would task UNMO teams to go to every incident. There was activity going on on the confrontation line, first light most mornings. There was a war going on, it was normal. Situation normal, Sarajevo, that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I was not quite on the same wavelength of you. I was thinking about the PTT building, because you know that at the time you shared this facility with others. That was the Sarajevo Sector we had there, we had the Bosnian liaison officers and you, the UNMOs. If you have any recollection about this matter, I'd like to know whether the week was agitated, busy or -- there, before the report of Mr. Alam, a report where he says that one should try to find a solution, an amicable solution with the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: The facts are that clearly the conflict was continuing, there was a lot of activity going on as there was every week. This might have been a heightened period of military activity. You're correct when you say the building was shared by a number of agencies. The BiH LOs were in the basement. We shared the building with the sector headquarter staffs. There clearly was friction with the BiH LOs after this incident and the way it was put across to them by Captain Hansen which led to further frustration and a belief that Captain Hansen might be made persona non grata and have to leave the mission, because that would have been completely unjust. People are always very sensitive and agitated when you are in a situation with deaths occurring daily and killings and everything else that was going on. But, no, there was no -- if you're trying to suggest there was any difficulty within the relationships inside the headquarters building, no there wasn't. Normal military activity, liaison carries on. I don't quite understand really what you're asking me, to be honest. I think we're on a different wavelength here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, we're on the same wavelength. You are the witness. I'm just asking you the question. You tell me about what you recollect. I'm not going to put any words in your mouth or in your mind. But it seems to me, when reading your report dated the 4th of July, we see that you're trying to calm the situation. Can you confirm that? You were trying to calm things down?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: That must be put in context. Clearly, I went to visit the same LOs later in the day from Thomas Hansen after this falling out had taken place, so I would have gone down with a fairly placatary manner to try and calm things down but the individuals we spoke to, and understandably, having taken the information the way it was given or the way they perceived it, were very angry and they were not going to be calmed down so I spent some time with them and then decided I wouldn't waste my time on them further and left. That's all there is to it. It is a straightforward situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you wrote on the 4th of July. You were trying to adopt a soothing tone. That's -- is that the same tone you adopted later on on the 4th of July, after all that time has elapsed after the conflict with Thomas Hansen, because your report seems to aim at calming things down.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Again, I have a disconnect here as to events and what it is you're leading to. You're absolutely correct; when I went down the same day as Captain Hansen clearly I was trying to placate or be conciliatory, calm down the LO that was making all these threats. That achieved nothing because he was very angry, and that terminated that meeting. Yes, the report was written on the 4th of July, recounting what had happened, but I don't think that changes anything. Could I just add -- and I think I can see some of the concern you have here. When you talk about Lieutenant-Colonel Alam's report and he talks about the dangers to UNMOs and things have to be resolved, anybody writing a report in English is only as good as the English they possess, and it is very difficult to read the right tone into a report written in a second language. And when I think Lieutenant-Colonel Alam refers to the dangers and having cooperation that that is just a standard concern of UN officers anywhere in the world on any mission, because unless you have full cooperation and unless you have freedom of movement you can't do your job. And therefore there is always a desire, being an impartial organisation, to have good relations with everybody, and that might have been a driving concern that affected some of the wording. As a native English speaker first language, I perhaps regard some of the tone slightly different to other people is what I'm saying. I don't read too much into this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that Mr. Thomas Hansen was refused access to Hrasnica, he was supposed to be impartial as an UNMO and right from the 1st of July, he was refused access?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes, and that is when the threats to make him persona non grata I suppose manifested themselves with reality, because that was the first occasion after a few days had elapsed that Captain Hansen tried to cross a confrontation line or through a check-point to go to the scene of an incident, and when it was established who he was, he was denied freedom of movement, so that illustrated to us that actually something formally had taken place and he had been restricted. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I was interrupted in my question, so I'll come back to the incident of the 1st of July, 1995. On that day, Mr. Hansen set out to carry out his regular duties, and he was refused access to part of the area controlled by the ABiH. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I don't recall that after 12 years in detail, other than reading it in the statements that I have been shown. But I am aware that happened, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But do you know that after all the conflict with the UNMOs had an impact on a house inhabited by the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand that question. When you say impacts, do you mean a munitions impact or a psychological impact?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm thinking about the impact of a projectile that struck the surroundings of a house inhabited by UNMOs on the 1st of July. Thomas Hansen set out to investigate and then he was refused access to the location where the incident had taken place. Apparently the surroundings of a house inhabited by UNMOs had been attacked. Do you remember that fact?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But from my recollection I don't think you need to put any weight on the fact that it was an UNMO house that suffered superficial damage. Any building in Sarajevo was fair game to every artillery round, mortar round, and tank round, so that was just the incident that caused Thomas Hansen to have to go and investigate when he had the issue about crossing through check-points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you say every building, you mean every building.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, potentially, sir, with the city being subjected to what it was over a period of time, clearly targeting may or may not be accurate and there is a possibility that any building could actually be struck, whether it is a block of flats, an official building, or a residence. So I don't think we put any emphasis on what particular building had been hit on any particular day. It is was just another incident, another shelling, another mortaring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And when you say fair game, fair game to whom? Do you mean to both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you mean fair game -- fair game, yes he did use the words "fair game." Fair game to whom? To both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all. I'm just trying to suggest that a round could impact anywhere and I don't think there was any particular issue as to what a round landed in. I'm trying to say that I don't think there was any particular relevance that that particular damage resulted at an UNMO house. It was just another building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the question put to you by His Honour Judge Robinson. Can you confirm that there was a war going on between the parties, between the warring factions in the areas where you were conducting your mission?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes. There was a confrontation line, drawn around Sarajevo with the Bosnian Serb forces on the outside and the BiH defending their territory on the inside and there were exchanges of fire regularly. For me, that is a war situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for me, too. I was stressing that matter for a specific reason, but I'll go back to this matter later on, because you say it is not relevant. We are talking about the 1st of July and following the discussion, the dispute with Mr. Hansen, there was this incident where an UNMO house was hit, maybe by chance. But I'd like to talk with you about the climate, the atmosphere that existed after this incident. Was the premature departure of Mr. Hansen not the price to pay to soothe down, to calm down the relationships between the LOs Mr. Salajdzic and Goro on the one hand and the UNMOs on the other hand, all these people being in the same building on a territory controlled by the ABiH. Was it not the price to pay?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: It may well have been but I would not have been part of any discussion to that effect or indeed to make any recommendations if that's what the UN command group decided. As an UNMO, this happened and at some point in time shortly afterwards, Captain Hansen was reposted within the mission so we accepted that he had been posted. That is the end of it for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But according to you, according to what you know, at the time Mr. Hansen was also a good UNMO officer, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes. Captain Hansen was very professional.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see any reason why yourself and Mr. Hansen and maybe any other UNMO, such as Captain [indiscernible] has invented such a story, made up such a story maybe to make Mr. Salajdzic, Mr. Goro angry as well as maybe the Bosnian government and maybe there was also another Salajdzic?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Again, I don't quite understand your question. If you're suggesting that there was an alternative agenda and people are making things up, that is an outrageous allegation. As UNMOs one reports what one sees with impartiality. That is all we do, no more, no less.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If this is the kind of translation you had, I don't understand either, and I will try to speak slowly and maybe I will try my English, if that can help. Do you and Mr. Hansen, the officer you mention as being a good officer, and UNMO the Kenyan officer, Mr. Idriz, at the time did you have any reason to make up this impact or the impact of a missile coming from the area controlled by the ABiH which struck a building on the territory controlled by the ABiH. Have you -- or did you have any reason to make it up?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, not -- one reports what one sees or what is what they believe they see. No more, no less.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And before I move on to something different, I would have liked the e-mail Mr. Hogan sent you to be tendered. Maybe we can see it. It is 65 ter 420D.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, did you get the translation? I was asking maybe we could have -- we could tender document 65 ter 42D, 420D, sorry, this is the e-mail that was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It is very faint. I'm not seeing it. Oh, that is the e-mail from Barry Hogan to the witness dated the 17th of September. Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have you asked questions about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have already asked a few questions and maybe I can continue before asking it to be tendered. I did ask a few questions and maybe the witness can confirm whether this is the e-mail that he did receive.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the e-mail that you did receive from Mr. Hogan?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D459, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, could you read paragraph -- we start with paragraph 1 would be the one that starts with "this particular shelling." And I would like you to read paragraph number 4, starting with: Is it possible."

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: 666 "Is it possible that the actual launch was from further out and that when you saw and heard the air bomb it was already in mid-flight, or is there no doubt in your mind about the launch being inside the lines?" And if I may, I responded to that e-mail, and I informed Mr. Barry Hogan that, yes, it is conceivable that the projectile was already in flight, and when the sound of a retort was heard that caused us to look left, north-westwards, we then visually picked up this projectile that was travelling slowly but may already have been in flight. That is, of course, a possibility, and we watched its trajectory either to the TV building or, I suppose, I would concede it might have gone behind it. Either way, it looked as though it went to the TV building and, then, as you know, from the reports a few seconds later there was a detonation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But what you're sure of is the direction the projectile came from. You're sure of that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm trying to consider whether you could be confronted with an optical illusion of something passing your frontage at an angle, it might appear to be a slightly different angle to what it really is. All I can say is that from my report -- or Captain Hansen's report that was an accurate account of events, that a projectile did pass that way, did head towards the TV building, may have gone into it, may have gone behind it, but either way within seconds, there was an explosion which clearly, being where we were, we assumed that it was the same event. That is all we thought we saw that morning. That is what we reported. And I was not aware, as I said to the Prosecution earlier, of all of the other reports at the time providing additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We should also admit the reply from the witness to Barry Hogan.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this has already been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Docherty, has it been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, that is the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, let me double-check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you remember you were shown the excerpts from Thomas Hansen's testimony on April 2nd this year. And you say that you were a bit surprised to learn that he said that he did not see it personally but that he only related what the two others -- two other UNMOs had told him on that day. You remember that, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I remember seeing the piece of paper, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But, on the other hand, you're telling us that your recollection is a bit blurry because 12 years have gone by. So could it be possible that you would be with Thomas Hansen on that parking lot but at another moment on -- of that day? Maybe when everything occurred, maybe a few minutes later, or maybe that you weren't with him, but then later you went with him to the parking lot on that very day. Do you think that is a possibility that you could envisage?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to the witness being invited to speculate in that way. I mean, Questions beginning with "is it possible," anything is possible. It's really just a form of giving testimony by counsel, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very surprised at this objection raised by the Prosecutor. This is a cross-examination. Both parties are cross-examining, so I think I can suggest something. This is a lesson that I learned from these proceedings. It's true that in my jurisdiction it's not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we said earlier, I was surprised when Captain Hansen's account said that: "We did not witness this together. My recollection is we were in the car park together however regardless of that, what I recall in terms of seeing the flight path of some sort of munitions and reporting it, as far as I recall, it is a fact now I would not be confused with that because I can remember it now sitting here, looking back across the city as we talk about it; so, no, I'm not confused by that. But I accept that maybe -- maybe Captain Hansen wasn't with me. Maybe it was another UNMO that was with me. I was not standing there on my own, but I don't recall exactly who it was. I'd always assumed over the last 12 years it was Captain Hansen, hence my surprise this morning. But I'm prepared to accept that it wasn't Captain Hansen."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now mention page 4372 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we could hand this over to the usher so that he could put this piece of paper on the ELMO so that the witness would see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And just disregard what I have highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, may I ask the witness to read it out loud so that everybody can have the translation into B/C/S, especially the accused in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he may do it.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I assume the witness is Captain Hansen, so Captain Hansen said: "We went to his car because his car was still parked outside. He came into the building, parked his car, for some reason he had something to do in the building. I don't know if it was to visit me or other business. So when he came to report this, we immediately went down to the car -- to his car to observe from the car, location, and he could point out from the direction from where this was fired."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, does this give you a reason why you -- you still have in mind the fact that you were on that parking lot with Mr. Hansen? Would that be the reason?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Certainly if that is what Captain Hansen had to say, then that supports the fact that he was inside, that he came down after the event and the incident was explained to Captain Hansen there and then, indicating and using directions. That is perfectly understandable. I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could I have my paper back?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now, since you were an eye-witness of what occurred that day, it is true that there was a real battle raging around the PTT building that day, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: No, there was not a real battle raging at all. There was obviously a number of events, a number of munitions being fired. That does not constitute a battle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the Prosecutor said that the offensive of the ABiH army had been launched and you didn't protest because this happened during an offensive that had been launched by the ABiH army. This is when this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: But you said a battle raging around the PTT. No, there was not a battle raging around the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I'm quite surprised. I didn't use such words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what came across in the translation, interpretation. Well, let's move on, and I believe you should be very near the end of your time now. You were allotted 1 hour and 10 minutes and we are just about 12 minutes from the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, absolutely. Could we please have document P42. We saw it earlier. It was shown earlier to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So now I'm going to ask a question to you as an officer. You're still in the army, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I'm still a serving officer in the Royal Air Force Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So I guess that you went through military training, military school, Military Academy. You did, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you're very competent in military matters and this is my question. During a war, sometimes the warring factions can boast about things that they never did to support the morale of troops, especially when troops are in dire straits during an offensive that has been launched by the opposing party. That could happen, right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: That is correct, it is theoretically possible that one side or the other could indulge in PSYOPS, psychological operations, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Wing Commander, if I may just put a little question to you regarding the exact location you were when you heard and saw the projectile. And my question is: Do you recall if you were on the upper or on the lower car park deck?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I think I would say the upper deck. I'm not 100 per cent sure but I seem to recall I was fairly close to the main building itself. My vantage point and that would have put me on the upper one, not the lower one. But I honestly -- it was the car park, I can't say, sir, I'm sorry, not with 100 per cent accuracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, it has some importance because I would imagine that your sight would have been obscured if you had been on the lower deck where I would assume most of the cars were parked because of the risk of shelling. So ...

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: No. I recall this event in the sense that one watched what was -- what was happening. At no point did I take cover, so whatever vantage point I had, I stood there and watched that projectile because that projectile presented no threat to me. I watched its path to my front by a few hundred metres which, again, the way I perceived it that day, struck the TV building or would have passed behind it, either way there was an explosion within seconds. Does that clarify that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, it does, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, you put some documents to the witness which we have already seen in the case. These are documents with -- in which the Serbs acknowledged that they hit the building that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to recall whether there was anything in it that identified a time when that took place. Did they identify a time when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The -- there are two answers to that. First of all, I think that the P42 from the accused gives at least a date but I would want to look at the text to be sure of that. But, secondly, from the evidence in this case I'm not aware of any other strikings on the TV building and so if we are talking -- so we're talking about a unique event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to go back to the witness now, because the witness said that in relation to that evidence, evidence from the Serbs themselves, acknowledging that they had hit the PTT building, he said that it may be that what he observed was a secondary event, and I asked him what he meant by secondary, and my recollection is that you said secondary to the -- to the -- whatever had been done by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Secondary or simultaneously, sir, having heard the fact that there is a ballistics report that fairly accurately identified where the damage, the scrapes or the impact was on the building, if clearly, the projectile I witnessed that morning did not cause the damage in the -- or the impact in the ballistics report, then I have to accept that as fact. And, therefore, all I was suggesting was that if the ballistics report shows damage to the south side or impact on the south, then the round I observed must have been a coincidental simultaneous event that may not have been the one that struck the TV building in accordance with the ballistics report; that is all I'm suggesting. Because I equally am now rather, I don't want to say confused but I am surprised that we seem to have simultaneous events or a ballistic report that does not match what I observed; and, therefore, in my mind I question whether the trajectory I observed was the one that clearly struck the south side of the building. And I don't see how it could have been. It must have been a simultaneous event otherwise I can't reconcile myself to what happened here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear any reports of any other -- any other hits on the building that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And again that has been troubling me as well and I have to say the answer to that is, no. I did not that day or in the following days read any other reports. However, to qualify that, we were all extremely busy, there were incidents happening all day, every day. And as soon as something would happen, you would be tasked with leading another investigation or sorting out another issue. So it is quite conceivable that although we reported what we report what happened we reported that morning, thereafter I was not involved in any other reports coming from other UNMOs or other agencies. And I just have to accept that that is the way it was conducted at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, may I draw your attention to your report dated the 4th of July on the incident of the 28th of June. We have looked at that report and it is in evidence. Is that the only report that you wrote on that -- on the incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir I believe it is because having gone up into the operations room after the incident, I would have reported what was seen, what we believe we saw that morning, that is why I also believe Captain Hansen was with me but I accept that could have been wrong. And then Captain Hansen translated that account of events into the report that we submitted and when he used the third person I just assumed that he was doing that for anonymity. Clearly if he wasn't there, the third person was correct and that was referring to myself. But there is no other report that is in evidence that is available for us to see today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you may have provided the answer to something that has been troubling me because in this report of yours on the 4th, there is no mention at all, no description at all of the -- of the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir. And what I'm suggesting is that the account that Thomas Hansen has signed off is the report that we made immediately after the incident. We would have gone back to the car park and point out directions and try and envisage where the projectile might have come from; and then subsequently, Captain Hansen as the duty operations officer would have written that report. Even, like you, I'm slightly surprised that there isn't a report that I physically wrote that morning because we would have gone up and compiled it together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So Captain Hansen would have immediately reported what you both saw and that's why you didn't have to write an individual report on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would have been reporting, sir, my account to him and, of course, he would have been down to the car park with me as per his transcript trying to work out the trajectory, the angle involved where the launch point might have been having had it explained to him. He obviously felt as a duty operations officer that he was then sufficiently knowledgeable to then draft the report of the facts as they were presented and send out it off under his signature. And I agree with you, the fact that I am not the signature block on that report is slightly surprising but Captain Hansen drafted it and sent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But that would then have meant that he was with you or you were with him, and the two of you witnessed this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was my thought initially and that was compounded in my mind when I read the report as though we'd both seen it. But I hear today now that Thomas Hansen maybe wasn't with me but came back down to have the incident described to him; then he drafted the report with my assistance on his signature block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have questions Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It is a Chamber witness, Your Honour. My questions would follow up on the questions that you were just asking but I do have a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Mindua first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, I have one last question regarding this projectile which you saw on June 28. You told us about this -- the signature, you said there was no smoke. Because of that, this led to you believe that there was no rocket attached to the projectile, at least at that point in time when you saw it. What conclusions can you draw, since you are an expert in weapons, about this weapon. Do you think that it is a projectile that is at the end of its trajectory, or is it a projectile that has no motor. In that case, could it be a mortar shell, a modified air bomb? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I am still unclear even today, sir, exactly what it was. I don't recall any kind of smoke signature behind the projectile as it went down its trajectory. It was fairly large, it was too big to be any kind of mortar round or even a small artillery shell or a larger artillery shell that would have been travelling with a different profile, unless it was in direct fire mode but it would have been travelling too fast. This projectile whatever it was was some, I would suggest improvised type device obviously being used in a method that it was not designed from. And wherever it was launched from, the initial launch would have provided it with its energy and then it seemed in a direct mode to be travelling horizontally under its own momentum until it impacted where it impacted. I do not recall a rocket motor being attached to this or if it had, it would have burnt out initially in the early phase of its flight and the rest was ballistic, but that all I can think sitting here 12 years on. I'm sorry, I can't be more precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said that it was a non-conventional projectile.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: We referred to this as an aerial bomb. I have not seen one that has not been fired on its launch point. I don't know exactly what they look like because those that were fired obviously detonated on impact. If the projectile that I observed was one of these aerial bombs that we talk about, all I know is in the trajectory I observed it was slow because one could track its path which you could not do with an artillery round or a heavier rocket with a motor. And therefore, it was a relatively sluggish slow moving device that was travelling north/south, loosely speaking, without any kind of rocket efflux coming out of the back of it at the point that I observed. I can't be more specific, I'm sorry, 12 years on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, how long will you be?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have any questions? How long.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Three and five, eight. I believe the interpreters can bear with us for another eight minutes. So we would just proceed, and then we would terminate the proceedings. We will not take the break now. You want to change your assessment from five minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give one minute, but Defence has something to start with, I think that the exhibit number given to the last number -- the last piece, is wrong, so we have a few logistics matters to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll just take the break. 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Docherty asks his questions, I would like to say that I have been informed that the document which I asked to be admitted and was told that it had been admitted, in fact it has not. This is the reply from Mr. Knowles to Barry Hogan dated 12th of September, and it's 65 ter 03510. So would that be admitted and given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes C16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And there's a correction to be made in relation to Exhibit D459.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That was document ID number DD 00-5132. That was mistakenly admitted as D459. The exhibit number should be D460.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I really just have something I want to clear up for purposes of the record not so much in the form of questions to the witness. In answering questions just before the break, the witness spoke about several things he learned this morning including impact on the south side of the building, and although did I it earlier in the proceedings, I want to make clear I'm not saying that the air bomb impacted the south side of the building and I just don't want the witness to misunderstand. Also, when the witness says the south side of the building, my point about the ballistics report not being consistent with an approach of the projectile from the north is based upon the marks on the roof. When we say the south side, I have not been to the TV building. Some people in this courtroom have and have gone done into this in much more detail but there is a small enclosed courtyard on the north side of the TV building and the blast damage was to the south wall of that inner courtyard. This is all in evidence in the trial. It doesn't change anything that I would have put to the witness, but I don't want the witness to have misunderstood or to think that I was saying something that's later shown not to be consistent with the evidence but it doesn't change any of the analysis that I have of the -- of the report. And as I said, I had no actual questions of the witness. I just wanted to clarify the record on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, let's just be clear about this, because I thought that the witness excluded a flight path from the north under the assumption that the building had been hit on its southern side but maybe the witness can testify to what he testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The witness can certainly, I'm sure speak to that. I just didn't want to get into the ballistics report in detail. I don't think Wing Commander Knowles had any role in the investigation. It was the subject of a lot of testimony. It is something that I think we are perhaps better off staying away from in detail with this witness. I just didn't want to be misunderstood as having elicited an answer from the witness by saying something that was not correct. And so when he spoke about impact I corrected that after the last break, and now after this break I just want to clarify that what I'm relying upon are these marks upon the roof. I do think it's quite clear-cut. We'll make submissions on that point of course. Just for purposes of today's proceedings I wanted to make clear what it was that I was saying when I said south. It is the south wall of the inner courtyard. And then one other item of business, Exhibit P940 and also the one that was just admitted, the other e-mail, again, because they have got internal e-mail addresses, could those please be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will be short. Maybe we're presenting things in a different matter and this is why I'm standing up to ask the question again, even though as Mr. Docherty says, everything is already in the file, in the case file. But if the witness is to give an opinion on this possibility, he must know that according to the investigation there was a ricochet impact. The expert of the Basim police made the analysis and there was not just one single impact. There were a number of impacts. I personally believe that we don't need to ask more questions but maybe you would like to know more about what happened, but I think we need to tell the witness exactly what the results of the Bosnian investigation was regarding the impacts on the tower. If you do not deem this useful, I can move on to something else. I have one last question. So it is up to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead with your one last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge asked you a question about your report of July 4th. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So let's be very clear on this. Your report dated July 4th, I'm going make a suggestion to you and you can say yes if you agree with me. This report is not on the investigation on the incident regarding the impact of the bomb but it relates to what happened between Hansen and the ABiH LOs, Silajdzic and Goro. That's the -- that's what your report is all about. You wrote the report about this incident, the dispute between Hansen and the LOs from the ABiH side.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: I believe there were two elements to that report and it is not front of us now but I think my wording was towards the end of that, that we -- I should go on to include the following about the -- the Captain Hansen element to that. There were two parts to that. Can we look at it again?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. This is document P519 on page 6.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at that now. I believe the first half of that report was I probably had been asked to just catalogue what happened that morning, and then at paragraph 6, I then go on to say additionally, on the 1st of July there occurred the following, so it seemed to me I had been asked to write that report actually to address the Captain Hansen earlier difficulties and then add it towards the end of that report what happened when he was denied access. I think there were two clearly halves to that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: There again, I'm not really sure. Maybe you did not understand my question in English. This is my question, I will repeat. You wrote a report on July 4th. According to me - and this is what I suggest - I believe that this was a report you wrote in the framework of an internal investigation regarding UNMOs after the very unpleasant situation which occurred between June 28, 1995, this very unpleasant situation that developed between the ABiH LOs and Thomas Hansen, which led to the fact that the ABiH army asking Mr. Hansen to be declared persona non grata. This is what you wrote the report about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW KNOWLES
utterances.text: It may well be. It just accounts what I would have been aware of regarding Captain Hansen and the difficulties with the BiH LOs or indeed subsequently his restriction on freedom of movement. I can't remember what document that has been extracted from. You would know. Either way it only covers my recollection of what happened with Captain Hansen. I accept it may well have been just a report into Captain Hansen's difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Wing commander, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave. We will be adjourning. We stand adjourned. Is there another issue? Oh, I see Ms. Isailovic has other issues. But the wing commander may leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. First a question that is connected to this witness but can be done without his presence. The document P846 was tendered by the Prosecution. This is a document, an UNMO document. It could have been relevant regarding this incident and everything that occurred around these dates. It is a report dated June 29 -- no, June 30th relating what occurred on June 29. The Prosecutor tendered this document but omitted to tender this document in its entirety, and I checked this with my colleagues. They did not tender the relevant pages of this document. So they tendered the document but everything that could be relevant regarding Sarajevo for our case does not exist in the e-court system, cannot be found in the documents that were disclosed to Defence and to the Bench. We would have wanted to have the document in its entirety, document which has already been admitted by the Bench. But as we have it now in e-court it is totally irrelevant and totally useless. If possible, we would like to have the document in its entirety. Otherwise, we will file a motion to obtain it but we believe that Prosecution can do what is necessary, so we can have the entirety of the report at our disposal. So this is my first point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Not yet, Mr. President I'm just looking to see what the document is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the document is on the screen now. This is supposedly an 18-page document. Unfortunately, we do not have the relevant pages that deal with Sarajevo and that deal with what occurred regarding UNMOs in Sarajevo, and Defence was really keen on getting these pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I was asking for the document to be brightened or to be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've got the document here, if you'd like. Got a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Admit it and tender it; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It says there are 18 page, page 1 of 18. And the question is: How much has been admitted and how much has not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eight pages are available, ten pages are missing, and unfortunately, the missing pages are related to Sarajevo and they relate to a very interesting time-period for the Defence. We realised it because this decision was admitted under your decision of the 29th of February, 2007. The document was admitted and received a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit evidence on the basis that the evidence is relevant and probative. So we need to satisfy ourselves about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm informed that we admitted the document in response to a motion by the Prosecutor to admit eight pages, and that's what we decided to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I'm not sure whether you are in a position to say what was it the intention of the Prosecution to confine the admission to eight pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour, but this is going back a way. You know, it was routine in this trial there were documents that were hundreds of pages long and either party would select a certain number of pages and put them in. If the other ten pages are also UNMO situation reports and if there are no Rule 70 issues, then I don't believe we would object. I'd like to see them first but if that's all that it is I don't see a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I'm afraid you will have to file a motion so we can examine the 12 pages and make a decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem is that the Prosecution is the one that controls the UN documents. They disclose what they want when they want it. Do you remember probably this series of very significant documents for the Defence and what happened. I have worked on the basis of the documents available in the system to find these ten pages. According to me, the rest of the document is not relevant, because it refers to Bihac Dubrovnik, therefore it might be relevant for other Trial Chambers, but this is not relevant for us. The date is extremely significant because we are talking about a selected number of incidents. We are talking about military activities and that's at the heart of the Defence case. Therefore, I believe it is completely unfair to submit and tender the documents that way by only tendering a few pages here and there. I remember that the Prosecution objected when we showed a number of documents, pages to witnesses. I see that the translation might not be up to standard, Mr. President, you may not be able to understand me. But what I wanted to say was that the Prosecution objected, and quite rightly so, when we tried to tender a number of documents where only part of a document had a been translated, and here, we have a document that is supposed to be a very relevant document in this case, and suddenly we realise that a number of pages are missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you be filing a motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are, of course, Your Honour. But I just wanted to point out that I do not have these ten missing pages. That is my problem. I don't have these pages. I'm in the hands of the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Assist to get these ten pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes. We tendered eight. We disclosed all of them on the 31th of the January. The Defence has got them. We'll give them to them again, but they've got them, and it is just incorrect to say that the OTP is doling out UN documents to suit our advantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You don't need to answer that because I believe that that is totally without any foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: We will redisclose these documents, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not disclosed, Prosecutor, because if it was the case, the document should be in the e-court system, should have been uploaded in the e-court system, when talking about fairness. There are number of pending issues related to documents that have not been tendered yet because the translation was missing. These are MFI documents, but they only have the status of MFI documents because at the time we did have a translation, it was not available. But now I'm very pleased to be able to tell that you we have received the translations of these documents. I can give you the relevant numbers for these documents to be admitted as exhibits proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you not file a motion on this issue? This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was something else. You see, we received the translations as soon they are ready and we proceeded the same way for the previous documents. Here we have documents that had been marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead with the --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D112 MFI, ID 00-1839, first document. Second document D146, ID DD00-0648. The following document, D246, then D297 and then D298. I would like to ask the Chamber to admit these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit them. Let me say something.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... earlier can you not file a motion on this -- I said have you not filed a motion on this. That's the question of MFIed documents. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last point the Defence would like to raise today is as follows. You made a ruling about the documents we submitted through Snezana Marinkovic Jekic, witness D-35. You ruled on some of the documents submitted through that witness. As I said, we receive the translations as soon as they are ready and I can tell you that we will be able to submit the translations tomorrow because tomorrow we'll have received all the translations, and we'd like to ask the Chamber to rule as quickly as possible about the admission of the documents that will be listed on that -- on that document, on that list. And that's all for administrative matters that the Defence wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, we had discussions earlier about the admissibility of some intercepts. You recall Ms. Isailovic brought our attention to that and we looked at the earlier transcripts, and I said to the Prosecutor Mr. Whiting that if he intends to rely on them, then he should bring a witness to speak to their authenticity. But as far as I'm aware, that has not been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as far as I'm aware, given the procedural stance of this case, that cannot be done and the reason I have not responded up to now is I am considering, given that we can't call a witness, whether to make a motion asking for the admission of these transcripts on the grounds that they are self-authenticating but that would take a little time and I didn't want to just do it off the cuff, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, I'm just informed in relation to the documents that I just admitted on your submissions, there are three of them in relation to which there is as yet no translation in the e-court system; D112, D297, and D298. So please attend to that as quickly as possible. It may be just a matter of getting them into the system.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we'll make sure that it is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We stand adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.15 p.m.
